cards.title: Types of taxes — Direct vs Indirect
cards.html:
Types of Taxes
  • Direct Taxes
    • Income TaxIncome Tax Act 2025
  • Indirect Taxes
    • Goods and Services Tax (GST)
    • Customs Duty

Direct tax

Mr X earns(1) job → salary (2) business (3) rent → house property (4) capital gain (gold sold) (5) other source (interest)
→
Pays tax directly
→
Government

Indirect tax

Mr X buys cloth1,000 + tax 180 = 1,180
→
Shop collects the tax
→
Governmentgets 180
  • Direct tax — paid by the person directly to the Government on his own income. Example: Income Tax (Income-tax Act, 2025).
  • Indirect tax — collected by a seller from the buyer and passed on to the Government. Examples: GST (Goods and Services Tax) and Customs Duty.

Sources of income on which income tax is paid (the five heads): (1) Job → Salary, (2) Business, (3) Rent → House Property, (4) Capital Gains (e.g. sale of gold), (5) Other Sources (e.g. interest income).

Indirect tax example (GST @18%):
Mr X buys cloth1,000
GST @18%180
Paid to shop1,180
Shop keeps 1,000 → pays 180 to Govt

Taxes fund public goods like roads and parks.

cards.title: Income-tax Act, 2025 — key facts
cards.html:
The levy of income-tax in India is governed by the Income-tax Act, 2025 (“the Act”).

  • It extends to the whole of India.
  • It came into force on 1st April, 2026.
  • It contains 23 chapters comprising 536 sections with 16 schedules.
  • Till 31.03.2026, income tax was governed by the Income-tax Act, 1961.
1-4-2025 to 31-3-2026→ old Act (1961)
1-4-2026 to 31-3-2027→ new Act (2025)

cards.title: Components of income tax law — what we will study
cards.html:
Income Tax 2025 — what we will study
  • 1. Income-tax Act, 2025
  • 2. Annual Finance Act
  • 3. Income-tax Rules, 2026
  • 4. Circulars and Notifications
  • 5. Legal Decisions
  1. Income-tax Act, 2025 — overview, important definitions, key provisions and sections.
  2. Annual Finance Act — Finance Act of the relevant year; amendments and new provisions. Every year the Finance Minister presents the Budget (1 Feb) and changes are made through the Finance Act (e.g. income up to ₹12 lakh → tax nil).
  3. Income-tax Rules, 2026 — overview, important rules and forms, compliance requirements, procedures and documentation.
  4. Circulars and Notifications — CBDT circulars, notifications and instructions, clarifications on provisions.
  5. Legal Decisions — important case laws and recent judgements.

cards.title: Basic terms
cards.html:
Basic Termscomponents of income tax law
  • Assessee
  • Tax Year
  • Assessment 2(13)
  • Person
  • Agricultural Income

The basic terms (components of income tax law): Assessee, Tax Year, Assessment [2(13)], Person and Agricultural Income.

How sections are read: Sec 1(i), Sec 1(ii), Sec 1(ii)(a) — section → sub-section → clause.

cards.title: Tax Year (Section 3) — IMPORTANT
cards.html:
Tax year1-4-2026 → 31-3-2027 · earn income
→
Next yearfrom 1-4-2027 · assessment (calculation)

Defined under section 3. It means the twelve months period of the financial year commencing on the 1st April. The income earned during the tax year is taxable after the end of that tax year.

  • If any business is started between the year, the tax year will be less than 12 months, but never more than 12 months.
Tax year: 1-4-2026 → 31-3-2027 (earn income)
Assessment: from 1-4-2027 (e.g. return by 31-7-2027) → calculation of tax

cards.title: Assessee (Section 2(11))
cards.html:
Assessee 2(11)a person by whom any tax or other sum of money is payable
  • (1) Proceedingevery person in respect of whom any proceeding has been taken
  • (2) Refund claimevery person who claims a refund
  • (3) Deemed assesseeevery person deemed to be an assessee under this Act

‘Assessee’ means a person by whom any tax or any other sum of money is payable under this Act. In addition it includes:

  1. Every person in respect of whom any proceeding under this Act has been taken.
  2. Every person who claims a refund.
  3. Every person who is deemed to be an assessee under this Act.

cards.title: Assessment (Section 2(13))
cards.html:
Income of an assessee
→
Determined (calculated) by the Assessing Officer
→
Includes reassessment & recomputation

The procedure by which the income of an assessee is determined (calculated) by the Assessing Officer (Income-tax Officer).

It includes reassessment and recomputation.

  2. Hindu Undivided Family (HUF)

cards.title: Individual
cards.html:
Individualonly a natural person — a human being
  • Male · Female · Child · Old man · Old woman
  • Minor / person of unsound mindassessment on the guardian or manager
  • Deceased personassessment on the legal representative

‘Individual’ means only a natural person, i.e. a human being — male, female, child, old man, old woman.

  • Includes a minor or a person of unsound mind.
  • In such cases, assessment may be made on the guardian or manager of the minor/lunatic who is entitled to receive his income.
  • In case of a deceased person, assessment is made on the legal representative.

cards.title: Hindu Undivided Family (HUF)
cards.html:
Hindu Undivided Family (HUF)separate entity · 'person' u/s 2(77)
  • Membersall males lineally descended from a common ancestor + their wives and daughters
  • Applicable toHindu, Jain, Sikh and Buddhist families
  • Head of the familyKarta
  • Under the Income-tax Act, 2025, a HUF is treated as a separate entity for assessment. It is included in the definition of ‘person’ u/s 2(77); the levy is on “every person”, so income-tax is payable by a HUF.
  • “HUF” is not defined under the Act. Under Hindu Law it is a family consisting of all males lineally descended from a common ancestor and includes their wives and daughters.
  • Applicable only to Hindu, Jain, Sikh and Buddhist families.
  • The head of the HUF (usually the eldest male) is the Karta.

cards.title: Schools of Hindu Law — Dayabhaga vs Mitakshara
cards.html:
Schools of Hindu Law
  • DayabhagaWest Bengal & Assam · right by succession, not by birth
  • Mitakshararest of India · right by birth, not by succession
BasisDayabhagaMitakshara
Prevalent inWest Bengal and AssamRest of India
DefinitionNobody acquires right/share in property by birth as long as the head of family is livingOne acquires right in family property by his birth, not by succession, even if elders are living
Right in propertyChildren acquire no share while the father is alive; only on the father’s deathEvery child born in the family acquires a right/share
CoparcenersThe father and his brothersAll male members up to four generations from a common ancestor
Key featureRight by succession, not by birthRight by birth, not by succession

cards.title: Company — classes
cards.html:
Classes of Companies
  • Domestic Company
    • Indian Company
  • Foreign Companya company which is not a domestic company

Company — Sec 2(20) of the Companies Act, 2013: incorporated under the 2013 Act or any previous company law (1956).

Definition (Sec 2(20), Companies Act, 2013): “Company” means a company incorporated under this Act (2013) or under any previous company law (e.g. Companies Act, 1956).

  • Domestic company — includes an Indian company.
  • Foreign company — a company which is not a domestic company.

cards.title: Partnership Firm
cards.html:
Partnership Firm
  • As defined u/s 4 of the Partnership Act, 1932registered firm
  • As defined u/s 2(1)(n) of the LLP Act, 2008

Partnership = relation between persons who have agreed to share the profits of a business carried on by all or any of them acting for all.

  • As defined u/s 4 of the Partnership Act, 1932 (registered firm), and
  • Limited Liability Partnership as defined u/s 2(1)(n) of the LLP Act, 2008.

Partnership is the relation between persons who have agreed to share the profits of a business carried on by all or any of them acting for all.

cards.title: Association of Persons (AOP)
cards.html:
Association of Persons (AOP)join for a joint enterprise, not a partnership in law
  • Common purpose or action
  • Main objectto produce income, not just to share it
  • Co-heirs, co-legatees, co-doneesjoining for a common purpose → AOP
  • ExampleMr X (individual) + Reliance Company start a new venture
  • When people combine for a joint enterprise and do not form a partnership in law, they are assessable as an AOP.
  • People must join for a common purpose or action.
  • Main object must be to produce income, not just to share it.
  • Co-heirs, co-legatees or co-donees joining together for a common purpose or action are also chargeable as an AOP.

Example: Mr X (individual) and Reliance Company together start a new venture for manufacturing electric vehicles → AOP.

cards.title: Body of Individuals (BOI)
cards.html:
Body of Individuals (BOI)two or more individuals earn income collectively
  • Only individualsunlike an AOP
  • Member's sharenot taxed again — BOI already paid the tax
  • ExampleMr A + Mr B start a cloth business for a short duration
  • A taxable unit of two or more individuals who join together for a common purpose and earn income collectively.
  • Includes only individuals, unlike an AOP which may include non-individual members.
  • Income-tax is not payable on the share of income received by a member from the BOI, as tax is already paid by the BOI.

Example: Mr A and Mr B (individuals) start a cloth-manufacturing business for a short duration without registering as a partnership → BOI.

cards.title: Difference between AOP and BOI
cards.html:
AOP vs BOI
  • AOPmembers: any person (individuals + company, firm) · come together voluntarily with a common will
  • BOImembers: only individuals · common will may or may not be present
BasisAOPBOI
MembersAny person — individuals as well as entities like company, firm etc.Only individuals; company, firm etc. cannot be members
Common willMembers voluntarily come together with a common will/intention or purposeCommon will may or may not be present

cards.title: Local Authority
cards.html:
Local Authority — examples
  • Municipal Committee
  • District Board
  • Body of Port Commissioners
  • Cantonment Board
  • Panchayat
  • Improvement Trust

Means a municipal committee, district board, body of port commissioners or other authority legally entitled to or entrusted by the Government with the control or management of a municipal or local fund.

Examples: Municipal Committee, District Board, Body of Port Commissioners, Cantonment Board, Panchayat, Improvement Trust.

cards.title: Artificial Juridical Persons
cards.html:
Artificial Juridical Personsnot natural persons · separate entities in law · residual category
  • Deities / Idols
  • Bar Council
  • Universities

Entities which are not natural persons but are separate entities in the eyes of law. Being a residual category, it covers all artificial persons with a juristic personality not falling under any other category of persons.

Examples: Deities/Idols, Bar Council, Universities.

cards.title: Income of a tax year assessed in the tax year itself (exceptions)
cards.html:
General Ruleincome of a tax year is assessed after the end of that tax year
  • Exceptions — assessed in the tax year itself
    • Shipping business of non-resident
    • Persons leaving India
    • AOP / BOI / AJP formed for a particular event or purpose
    • Persons likely to transfer property to avoid tax
    • Discontinued business

General rule: income of a tax year is assessed after the end of that tax year (tax year → earn → next year → assessment).

Exceptions — income assessed in the tax year itself:

  1. Shipping business of a non-resident
  2. Persons leaving India
  3. AOP / BOI / Artificial Juridical Person formed for a particular event or purpose
  4. Persons likely to transfer property to avoid tax
  5. Discontinued business

Next topic: income tax rates.

cards.q: Define 'Tax Year' under the Income-tax Act, 2025. Can a tax year be more or less than 12 months?
cards.a:
Tax year is defined under section 3: the twelve-month period of the financial year commencing on 1st April. Income earned during the tax year is taxable after the end of that tax year.

It can be less than 12 months (e.g. a business started during the year — the tax year runs from the date of commencement to 31st March) but never more than 12 months.

cards.q: Who is an 'Assessee' under section 2(11)?
cards.a:
A person by whom any tax or other sum of money is payable under the Act. It also includes:

  1. every person in respect of whom any proceeding under the Act has been taken;
  2. every person claiming a refund;
  3. every person deemed to be an assessee under the Act.

cards.q: What is 'Assessment' under section 2(13)?
cards.a: The procedure by which the income of an assessee is determined by the Assessing Officer. It includes reassessment and recomputation.

cards.q: Name the categories of 'Person' under section 2(77).
cards.a:
1. Individual
  2. Hindu Undivided Family (HUF)
  3. Company
  4. Firm
  5. Association of Persons (AOP) / Body of Individuals (BOI)
  6. Local Authority
  7. Artificial Juridical Person

cards.q: Distinguish between an AOP and a BOI with examples.
cards.a:

MembersAny person — individuals, companies, firmsOnly individuals

AOP example: Mr X and Reliance Company jointly start an EV-manufacturing venture.

BOI example: Mr A and Mr B (individuals) jointly run a cloth business for a short time without registering a partnership.

cards.q: When is the income of a tax year assessed in the tax year itself?
cards.a:
General rule: income is assessed after the end of the tax year. Exceptions:

  1. Shipping business of a non-resident
  2. Persons leaving India
  3. AOP/BOI/Artificial Juridical Person formed for a particular event or purpose
  4. Persons likely to transfer property to avoid tax
  5. Discontinued business

cards.q: State any four key facts about the Income-tax Act, 2025.
cards.a:
• Extends to the whole of India.
  • Came into force on 1st April 2026.
  • Has 23 chapters, 536 sections and 16 schedules.
  • Replaced the Income-tax Act, 1961, which applied till 31.03.2026.

cards.title: The five heads of income (with examples)
cards.html:
Total Income — 5 heads
  • Salariesjob (employee ← employer)
  • House Propertyrent
  • Business or Profession (PGBP)shop, business, service
  • Capital Gainssale of gold, shares…
  • Other SourcesFD interest, lottery…
  1. Salaries — Mr Ram (employee, EE) works for XYZ Ltd (employer, ER) → salary (rules: sec 17).
  2. Income from House Property — rent from letting out a house.
  3. Profits and Gains of Business or Profession (PGBP) — profit from a shop/business or from rendering a service/profession.
  4. Capital Gains — gain on sale of a capital asset, e.g. 2 kg gold bought for ₹2L sold for ₹2cr (gain ₹1.98cr); 1,000 Reliance shares bought for ₹20L sold for ₹45L (gain ₹25L).
  5. Income from Other Sources — bank FD interest, lottery, Dream11 winnings, crypto profits, etc.

cards.q: Distinguish between basic (slab/flat) rates and special rates of income tax.
cards.a:
• Basic rates are fixed every year by the Finance Act. Individuals, HUFs, AOPs, BOIs and AJPs pay slab rates; companies, firms and local authorities pay flat rates.
  • Special rates are laid down in the Income-tax Act itself for specific incomes — capital gains (STCG on shares 20%, LTCG 12.5%), lottery/crossword/races/gambling/online games/VDA (30%), deemed income (30%).

cards.html:
New Tax Regime

Under the new tax regime (default, Section 202) the assessee follows a different set of:

  • Tax rates — a single slab rate for everyone (no separate senior/super-senior slabs)
  • Deductions (Chapter VIII) — mostly not allowed
  • Income — special-rate incomes are still taxed at their special rates; the rest at the new slabs

To use the old regime, the assessee must opt out of the new regime u/s 202.

cards.title: Surcharge — tax on tax
cards.html:
Surchargeon tax
  • Old Regime

Tax
→
+ Surcharge (on tax)
→
+ 4% cess on (tax + surcharge)
→
= Tax liability

Surcharge is levied on the income-tax amount (not on income) when total income exceeds ₹50 lakh. Cess is then charged at 4% on (tax + surcharge).

  • Special income — STCG on shares (sec 196), LTCG other assets (197), LTCG shares (198) and dividend income — surcharge capped at 15%.

cards.title: Marginal relief on surcharge
cards.html:
Income crosses a surcharge threshold slightly
→
Extra tax + surcharge ≤ extra income
→
Marginal relief = the excess

When income crosses a surcharge threshold by a small amount, the extra tax + surcharge cannot exceed the extra income above the threshold.

Marginal relief = Total tax liability (incl. surcharge)
− Tax on threshold income (incl. its surcharge)
− Extra income over threshold

cards.q: Explain the surcharge rates applicable to individuals and the cap on special incomes.
cards.a: Surcharge is a percentage of income-tax: 10% (₹50L–1cr), 15% (₹1–2cr), 25% (₹2–5cr), 37% above ₹5cr in the old regime (capped at 25% in the new regime). For the 25%/37% bands income is measured excluding dividend and capital gains u/s 196–198. On tax on dividend and capital gains u/s 196–198 the surcharge cannot exceed 15%. Marginal relief ensures the extra tax plus surcharge on crossing a threshold does not exceed the extra income.
